newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Dollar claws back losses in Asia, bonds firmer.
newsitem.headline: Dollar claws back losses in Asia, bonds firmer.

text.p: The dollar clawed back overnight losses in Asian trading on Wednesday and regional bond markets were firmer following the U.S. Federal Reserve Board's decision to leave interest rates unchanged, dealers said.

At 0420 GMT the dollar was quoted at 109.65/75 yen, having touched a low in Asia of 109.29 yen. Immediately before the overnight news of the Fed's decision, it had been trading in the United States at 109.80/83 yen.
The dollar fell initially as many dealers had expected the Fed to raise interest rates by at least 25 basis points.
The Federal funds rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans was left at 5-1/4 percent and the discount rate the Fed charges banks for loans stayed at five percent.
However, Tokyo foreign exchange dealers said Japanese importers had taken the opportunity to snap up what they saw as cheap dollars for their future overseas investments.
"This has been the recent pattern -- the dollar falls overseas and then meets strong buying interest from Japanese operators in Tokyo," said a Tokyo dealer with a European bank.
The head of trading at a European bank in Singapore -- who had expected the Fed to raise rates -- said he thought it had made a mistake in not doing so.

"There has to be a very weak series of numbers (economic data) to back up their inaction. I think the fact they didn't move overnight could mean they'll have to raise rates by 1/2 point later. A 1/4 now could have nipped that in the bud," he said.
"When the minutes come out (on November 15) they will definitely show dissention amongst the Fed members," he said.

He said he did not expect the dollar to be weakened by the Fed's inaction. "You can see it creeping back up right now," he said. "Selling dollars has proved a very expensive thing to do recently and I don't see that changing," he said.

The head of Treasury at another bank in Singapore commented, "The lack of a move from the Fed didn't help me at all to be quite honest. If the stories are true, the majority of the 12 Fed members wanted a raise in rates. I can't help but feel that (Federal Reserve chief) Greenspan is behind this."
In the bond markets prices rose initially on the back of a rally in the U.S. treasury market after the news, but later came back as treasuries slipped back in Tokyo.
At 0420 GMT the benchmark U.S. 30-year long bond was quoted at 96-28/32 pct in Tokyo to yield 7.00 percent. This compares with a New York close of 97-1/32 pct.
The head of trading at the European bank in Singapore forecast the long bond yield could climb to 7.25 percent as the market began to price in a future Fed tightening.
"The higher (Treasury) yields will be another factor supporting the dollar," he said.
Australian bonds rallied on the news of the Fed's inaction since it meant the yield premium of Australian bonds over U.S. bonds remained intact. They later slipped back slightly.
Traders in Sydney said they would now be looking at domestic factors -- such as forthcoming consmuer price index and wages data -- to predict market direction.
Japanese bond markets were also more focussed on domestic matters.

Kunihoro Ishibashi, manager of the bond department at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, said the Japanese government bond market rose slightly on the Fed news, but was more concerned about the results of a 10-year bond auction later on Wednesday.
"Moves in U.S. interest rates have little impact on the market here...as Japan is not facing any inflationary risk at the moment and is not in a situation to raise rates anyway," he said.
